summary:
Kurgan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full and with no identified regional deviation. The dedicated country record identified no deviation material enough to score separately (±0.02), so the oblast is assessed at the national score.

For a trans visitor this framework means that legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; gender-transition procedures are banned and gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation operates nationwide, including in Kurgan Oblast: participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 of them administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The 2013 "propaganda" law, expanded in 2022 to cover any public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition, is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the two preceding years.

Foreigners are explicitly at risk. The US State Department advisory for Russia states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and it advises against all travel to Russia; the advisory stands at Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Kurgan Oblast is not a local phenomenon but one strand of a national wave. The 101 extremism-related convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch by 30 June 2025 were entered by courts across the country under both the administrative and criminal codes, and the eighteenfold rise in propaganda-law cases over the decade reported by Meduza reflects nationwide charging practice rather than oblast policy.

The penalties attached to display are worth separating from those attached to identity. Carrying or showing a rainbow flag falls under article 20.3 as displaying banned symbols and produced 81 convictions in 98 administrative cases between January 2024 and June 2025, whereas participation in or organisation of the designated movement is charged as a criminal offence carrying years of imprisonment.

Official warnings to travellers exist in parallel with official hostility. The US State Department's Level 4 advisory and the UK Home Office's country policy note both describe risk to LGBT travellers in Russia directly, and Human Rights Watch has asked governments to offer safe haven to people leaving the country, which places a trans visitor's exit options alongside their entry risk.

The nearest comparable documented cases are drawn from other Russian cities rather than from Kurgan Oblast itself: the Moscow bar raids of January 2024, the St Petersburg account published in June 2025, and the conversion-therapy detention of a trans woman near Novosibirsk in 2021. They indicate the pattern of enforcement and private coercion that the oblast's residents and visitors stand under.

Residents of Kurgan Oblast live under the same national statutes as visitors, with two aggravating features. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are unavailable rather than merely restricted, so a resident who has not already changed documents has no domestic route to do so; gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited outright.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution and that the state is able but unwilling to protect them. It records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Residents charged under the extremist designation face a materially heavier exposure than the administrative propaganda provisions: participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising six to ten years, and three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 face up to 12 years. A resident detained on such charges has already been reported dead in a pretrial detention facility in a separate December 2024 case.

Coercive conversion practice is documented against transgender residents. A transgender woman was held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre to which relatives lured her in summer 2021, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, and escaped only after police responded to a phone she had found.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kurgan-Oblast-specific enforcement record is sourced in this inventory. There is no oblast-level reporting on raids, extremism charges, propaganda-law fines or detentions; the documented cases cited here originate in Moscow, St Petersburg and the Novosibirsk area, and are used as indicators of the national pattern the oblast stands under.

The claim that no regional deviation from the national position was identified rests on a scoring tolerance of ±0.02 rather than on a survey of oblast practice. Whether local police, courts or medical providers in Kurgan Oblast apply the national framework more or less rigorously than the national average is unresolved.

The availability of gender-affirming care in Kurgan Oblast specifically, and the treatment of transgender visitors at border or document checks in this oblast, are not sourced and remain unresolved. The reported 2023 ban is stated at the national level.

The counting basis for the 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 is the UK Home Office's own figure; the inventory does not break it down by charge type or by region.
